answer: The network caps how much any single account can take per epoch, so even a cleverly large farm cannot monopolize one epoch's rewards — the surplus is spread across many passing identities. The reason this works is that the attacker must pay a real cost on every identity, so scale becomes a liability rather than an advantage. In effect, the network makes cheating the most expensive strategy available, which is the closest thing to a Sybil-resistant design that economics allows. Consider a wander as the anchor of the cost.
